Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Specific lexico-semantic predictions are associated with unique spatial and temporal patterns of neural activity" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by Joshua Gold as Senior Editor and a Reviewing Editor. The reviewing editor writes:

I've now read the manuscript and author rebuttal in detail and I'm pleased to see that the authors have addressed the technical and methodological challenges that were raised by the reviewers of the original manuscript. I'm now satisfied that the results establish that information conveyed by a predictable sentence final word is activated at an early stage during processing of the penultimate word in a sentence. I think that this finding makes an important contribution to the literature by more-firmly establishing early lexical-semantic activation of predicted words as a key property of human sentence processing, and demonstrating a novel method by which the these time-limited lexical-semantic predictions can be shown in neural data.

While the manuscript has been much improved there are two remaining issues that I think need to be addressed before acceptance, as outlined below:

1) There are too many places in the Introduction and Discussion in which I think the authors aren't thinking critically enough about whether it is only their preferred "generative and predictive" view that could explain the present findings. My view is that many other accounts could also explain their findings. Specifically, any model which: (i) activates a cumulative semantic representation of sentence meaning, and (ii) emphasises processing speed and efficiency such that semantic representations that are strongly implied by the words read so far, but not yet directly expressed in words are activated – can also account for the current findings. There are many such models in the literature, but most notable (to my mind) is the "sentence gestalt" model from St John and McClelland, 1990, that has been recently updated by Rabovsky et al., 2018, and can predict the magnitude of EEG N400 responses in a wide range of sentence processing paradigms. To my knowledge this is not a model which is explicitly "generative and predictive" and yet I think it very likely that RSA analysis of the sentence gestalt representations generated by this model could simulate the results of the present study. While I don't think that the authors need to do the work to explore whether the model *can* simulate their findings, I do think that it is in their interests to offer a more balanced overview of the literature and to more precisely explain what sort of computational model is implied by their findings.

2) I had one other minor question about the method that they used in comparing cloze probabilities between and within item pairs which could be addressed by same time. This point is described in more detail in their rebuttal letter than in the manuscript. However, I think that this issue deserves a little more attention in the manuscript given the known importance of cloze probability in predicting the magnitude of EEG/MEG signals during sentence processing, and the. Specifically, in the rebuttal letter the authors report analyses of the difference between cloze probability for sentence pairs. However, if my understanding of this analysis is correct this analysis should be conducted not on the difference between cloze probabilities, but rather the absolute difference between cloze probabilities for within and between item pairs. I think that otherwise the average difference between cloze values would always be zero. I'd like the authors to report this analysis in the manuscript, including a description of the method used for conducting the analysis.

claims.source: We interpret this finding as reflecting the greater spatial similarity in the pattern of brain activity produced by the prediction of the same word than the prediction of a different word.
claims.evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their main finding.

claims.claim: The spatial similarity effect only became apparent after the onset of the word immediately preceding the SFW (i.e. after the SFW-1), suggesting it is unlikely to have reflected any general differences in the full contexts.
claims.source: The fact that the spatial similarity effect only became apparent after the onset of the word immediately preceding the SFW (i.e. after the SFW-1) suggests that it is unlikely to have reflected any general differences in these contexts (the full set of words prior to the SFW).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the timing of the observed effect.

claims.claim: The observed spatial similarity effect reflects the prediction of the SFW rather than lexical processing of the SFW-1.
claims.source: This strongly suggests that the observed effect reflects the prediction of the SFW rather than lexical processing of the SFW-1.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the control analysis with matched SFW-1.

claims.claim: The increased spatial similarity detected in the within-pair sentences reflects activity related to the prediction of a specific SFW.
claims.source: A second set of alternative interpretations might acknowledge that the increase in spatial similarity detected in the within-pair sentences reflects activity related to the prediction of a specific SFW.
claims.evidence: This is the authors' favored interpretation of their findings.

claims.claim: Several previous studies have reported evidence of anticipatory lexico-semantic processing following constraining relative to non-constraining contexts.
claims.source: This is by no means the first study to show evidence of lexico-semantic prediction before the onset of new bottom-up input during sentence processing. Several previous studies have reported evidence of such anticipatory processing following constraining relative to non-constraining contexts (see Kuperberg and Jaeger, 2016a, section 3.1), at least under experimental conditions that encourage the generation of high-certainty lexico-semantic predictions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claims.claim: The present study provides neural evidence that lexico-semantic predictions are item-specific – different predicted words are associated with spatially distinct patterns of neural activity.
claims.source: What distinguishes the present study from this previous work is that it provides neural evidence that these lexico-semantic predictions are item-specific – that is, different predicted words are associated with spatially distinct patterns of neural activity.
claims.evidence: This is the authors' statement of the novel contribution of their study.

claims.claim: Nouns and verbs are known to have distinct neuroanatomical representations.
claims.source: This is because we designed our study such that 50% of the predicted SFWs were nouns and 50% were verbs, allowing us to calculate the within-category spatial similarity between all pairs of sentences that predicted the same syntactic category. We compared these within-category spatial similarity values with the within-pair spatial similarity values, in which the predicted SFWs shared both syntactic category and lexico-semantic features. We found that the within-category spatial similarity values were significantly smaller than the within-pair spatial similarity values (Figure 2—figure supplement 4). These findings suggest that the within-pair spatial similarity effect did not simply reflect the prediction of the broad syntactic category of the SFW.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge cited in the context of interpreting the results.

claims.claim: The spatial similarity effect reflected similarities at the level of the semantic properties and features that defined the meanings of the predicted words.
claims.source: Instead, we suggest that the spatial similarity effect reflected similarities at the level of the semantic properties and features that defined the meanings of the predicted words.
claims.evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their findings.

claims.claim: The prediction of the particular set of semantic properties and features corresponding to a word may be reflected by the activation of a particular spatially distributed network.
claims.source: For example, the prediction of the particular set of semantic properties and features corresponding to the word <baby> (e.g. <human>, <small>, <cries>) may have been reflected by the activation of a particular spatially distributed network that differed from the network reflecting the prediction of the particular set of semantic features corresponding to a different predicted word, <roses> (e.g. <plant>, <scalloped petals>, <fragrant smell>).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of how semantic features might be represented.

claims.claim: The increased spatial similarity in association with sentence pairs that predicted the same word may have reflected similarities of predictions generated at a lower phonological and/or orthographic level of representation.
claims.source: It is also possible that the increased spatial similarity in association with sentence pairs that predicted the same word reflected similarities of predictions generated at a lower phonological and/or orthographic level of representation.
claims.evidence: This is an alternative interpretation considered by the authors.

claims.claim: The prediction of semantic features may lead to the top-down pre-activation of information at lower phonological and/or orthographic levels of the linguistic hierarchy.
claims.source: On this account, the prediction of semantic features led to the top-down pre-activation of information at these lower levels of the linguistic hierarchy before new bottom-up information became available to these levels (see Kuperberg and Jaeger, 2016a, sections 3 and 5 for discussion).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical account cited from previous work.

claims.claim: The spatial similarity effect began at 120 ms after the onset of the word before the predicted SFW (i.e. SFW-1), providing evidence that the prediction of the SFW was generated at the first point in time at which participants had sufficient information to unambiguously generate this prediction.
claims.source: As noted above, the spatial similarity effect began at 120 ms after the onset of the word before the predicted SFW (i.e. SFW-1), even though the effect was not driven by the lexical properties or the predictability of the SFW-1 itself. This provides evidence that the prediction of the SFW was generated at the first point in time at which participants had sufficient information to unambiguously generate this prediction.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the timing of the effect.

claims.claim: Following highly constraining contexts, comprehenders are able to predict entire events or states, along with their associated semantic features, prior to the appearance of new bottom-up input.
claims.source: This type of account follows from a generative framework of language comprehension in which, following highly constraining contexts, comprehenders are able to predict entire events or states, along with their associated semantic features, prior to the appearance of new bottom-up input (e.g. Kuperberg and Jaeger, 2016a, sections 4 and 5; Kuperberg, 2016b; St. John and McClelland, 1990; Rabovsky et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical framework cited from previous work.

claims.claim: The spatial similarity effect primarily reflects similarities at the level of semantic features associated with the predicted word, rather than similarities of the entire predicted events/states.
claims.source: Importantly, however, we conceive of the spatial similarity effect detected here as primarily reflecting similarities at the level of semantic features (e.g. <human>, <small>, <crying>) associated with the predicted word ('baby'), rather than similarities of the entire predicted events/states (e.g. the <baby sleeping in the crib> event versus the <newborn baby in the hospital> event) (see Kuperberg, 2016b).
claims.evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of what level of representation their effect reflects.

claims.claim: The spatial similarity effect lasted until 515 ms following the onset of the SFW-1 and then dropped off in the second half of the interval before the onset of the SFW.
claims.source: Despite its early onset, the spatial similarity effect was fairly short-lived: it lasted until 515 ms following the onset of the SFW-1 (corresponding to 315 ms following its offset at 200 ms), and then dropped off in the second half of the interval before the onset of the SFW (see Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of the spatial similarity effect shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: It is possible that the predicted information was not maintained over the relatively long interstimulus interval used in the present study (SOA: 1000 ms per word).
claims.source: It is possible that, the predicted information was not maintained over the relatively long interstimulus interval used in the present study (SOA: 1000 ms per word).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of why the effect was transient.

claims.claim: Representations within working memory can be maintained in a silent neural state, instead of being accompanied by persistent delayed activity.
claims.source: This idea has been recently discussed in relation to the notion of 'activity-silent' working memory, which holds that representations within working memory can be maintained in a silent neural state, instead of being accompanied by persistent delayed activity (Stokes, 2015b; Wolff et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical concept cited from previous work.

claims.claim: The unique spatial pattern of brain activity associated with the prediction of specific words changed over time.
claims.source: This suggests that the unique spatial pattern of brain activity associated with the prediction of specific words changed over time.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cross-temporal spatial similarity analysis.

claims.claim: Different semantic features associated with the prediction of a specific word might have been recruited at different time points.
claims.source: We speculate that this may be because different properties associated with particular words became available at different times. For example, the different semantic features (e.g. <human>, <small>, <cries>) associated with the prediction of a specific word (e.g. 'baby') might have been recruited at different time points.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the dynamic spatial patterns.

claims.claim: The prediction of specific words was associated with unique temporal patterns of neural activity.
claims.source: In addition to being associated with unique spatial patterns of neural activity, we also found evidence that the prediction of specific words was associated with unique temporal patterns of neural activity.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the temporal RSA findings.

claims.claim: A recent study applying temporal RSA to intracranial EEG signals reported that the temporal pattern of neural activity within the left inferior temporal lobe encoded item-specific representations during picture naming.
claims.source: This observation is in line with a recent study that applied temporal RSA to intracranial EEG signals, and reported that the temporal pattern of neural activity within the left inferior temporal lobe encoded item-specific representations during picture naming (Chen et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Temporal similarity patterns corresponding to unique lexico-semantic items can be detected before new bottom-up input becomes available.
claims.source: The current findings extend these previous results by suggesting that temporal similarity patterns corresponding to unique lexico-semantic items can be detected before new bottom-up input becomes available.
claims.evidence: This is the authors' statement of how their findings extend previous work.

claims.claim: Damasio (1989) proposed that multimodal semantic features become bound together through a process of 'temporal synchrony' within 'convergence zones'.
claims.source: However, we suggest that it is consistent with a classic theory by Damasio (1989), who proposed that multimodal semantic features, represented in widely distributed regions of the cortex, become bound together through a process of 'temporal synchrony', and that this binding occurs within 'convergence zones', which act to unify these features into a discrete whole (Damasio, 1989).
claims.evidence: This is a citation to a classic theoretical proposal.

claims.claim: The unique temporal patterns of neural activity within the left ventral/medial temporal lobe may have played a functional role in binding the unique sets of semantic features represented by the unique spatial patterns of neural activity.
claims.source: In the present study, it is possible that the unique temporal patterns of neural activity within the left ventral/medial temporal lobe played a functional role in binding the unique sets of semantic features that were represented by the unique spatial patterns of neural activity.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional role of the temporal patterns.

claims.claim: The unique temporal patterns of neural activity may have played a role in binding semantic information as it became available dynamically over time.
claims.source: Speculatively, these unique temporal patterns of neural activity may have also played a role in binding this information as it became available dynamically over time (as opposed to becoming available all at once).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the temporal binding mechanism.

claims.claim: A particular temporal signature may have functioned to bind the dynamically evolving and spatially distributed pattern of neural activity into a coherent lexico-semantic representation.
claims.source: For example, by tracking (or perhaps even orchestrating) the particular time-course of accessing the distributed brain regions that represent the semantic features of <baby> (e.g. <human>, <small> and <cries>), a particular temporal signature may have functioned to bind the dynamically evolving and spatially distributed pattern of neural activity into a coherent lexico-semantic representation, corresponding to participants' subjective experiences of predicting a specific word.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of how temporal binding might work.

claims.claim: The localization of the temporal similarity effect to the left ventral temporal regions is consistent with the well-established role of these regions in lexico-semantic processing.
claims.source: The localization of the temporal similarity effect to the left ventral temporal regions (left inferior temporal lobe and fusiform cortex) is consistent with the well-established role of these regions in lexico-semantic processing (Lüders et al., 1991; Lüders et al., 1986; McCarthy et al., 1995; Mummery et al., 1999; Nobre and McCarthy, 1995; Visser et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The left ventral temporal regions have been proposed to function as 'hubs' that bring together widely distributed semantic features across the cortex.
claims.source: In particular, it is consistent with the proposed role of these regions as 'hubs' that brings together widely distributed semantic features across the cortex (Patterson et al., 2007; Ralph et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claims.claim: Semantic hubs may function as a 'dictionary' by mediating between widely distributed conceptual knowledge and specific word forms.
claims.source: Such hubs may function as a 'dictionary' by mediating between widely distributed conceptual knowledge and specific word forms (orthographic and phonological knowledge) (Caramazza, 1996; Damasio et al., 1996) and/or they play a more domain-general role in semantic processing (Nobre et al., 1994; Patterson et al., 2007; Reddy and Kanwisher, 2006; Shimotake et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical and empirical work.

claims.claim: The hippocampus plays a crucial role in binding representations to generate predictions.
claims.source: While MEG source-modeling results within medial and subcortical regions should be interpreted with caution, the possible involvement of the hippocampus is interesting given other work that has implicated it as playing a crucial role in binding representations to generate predictions.

claims.source: A large literature from recordings in rats demonstrates that the hippocampus represents upcoming spatial representations as the rat is navigating (Gupta et al., 2012), and we have a good understanding of the physiological mechanisms supporting such predictions (Lisman and Redish, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous animal studies.

claims.source: Moreover, recently, it was found that the temporal patterns in higher frequency bands recorded within the hippocampus were similar between a pre-picture interval and the picture itself (Jafarpour et al., 2017), suggesting a role in representing pre-activated non-verbal semantic information.

claims.source: Indeed, Piai et al. (2016) used intracranial recordings in humans to demonstrate predictive effects in the hippocampus in a language task in which the sentence-final word had to be produced (Piai et al., 2016).

claims.evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claims.source: In the present study, we deliberately used highly constraining contexts to encourage participants to generate high certainty specific lexico-semantic predictions, and we used a long interstimulus interval between words to ensure that we would be able to detect any representationally specific neural activity if it was present.

claims.claim: When item-specific lexico-semantic predictions are generated, they are associated with unique spatial and temporal patterns of neural activity.
claims.source: We see the unique contribution of our study as providing evidence that, when we know that item-specific lexico-semantic are generated, they are associated with unique spatial and temporal patterns of neural activity.

results.result: The study used MEG to measure brain activity while 26 participants read 240 highly constraining sentences presented at 1000 ms per word. Sentences were constructed in 120 pairs that predicted the same final word despite different contexts, with pair members separated by at least 30 sentences during presentation. Comprehension accuracy was high (98% ± 2.0%).
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C21-C25, C27-C29 collectively describe the experimental design and basic behavioral results. The methodology is clearly described with appropriate detail, and the high comprehension accuracy (C29) validates that participants engaged with the task. The design is well-suited to test the hypothesis about item-specific predictions.

results.result: Spatial RSA revealed that the spatial pattern of MEG activity was more similar when sentence pairs predicted the same word (within-pairs) versus different words (between-pairs) in the time window 120-515 ms after the penultimate word onset (−880 to −485 ms before the final word; t(25) = 3.751, p < 0.001). This effect was present in 18/26 participants and was not observed at earlier time windows.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C30-C34, C46 describe the main spatial RSA finding with appropriate statistical support. The effect is statistically significant, shows consistency across most participants (C33), and demonstrates temporal specificity (C34 shows no effect at earlier time windows). The timing and magnitude of the effect are clearly documented.

results.result: The spatial similarity effect cannot be explained by differences in the number of within-pair versus between-pair comparisons. A control analysis using matched numbers of comparisons confirmed the effect (t(25) = 2.393, p = 0.025).
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36 address a potential methodological confound. The statistical argument in C35 is sound, and the control analysis in C36 provides empirical confirmation. The effect remains significant even when controlling for the number of comparisons, strengthening the main finding.

results.result: The spatial similarity effect reflects prediction of the final word rather than lexical processing of the penultimate word (SFW-1). Lexical properties and predictability of SFW-1 were matched between within-pair and between-pair sentences. A control analysis with matched SFW-1 showed the effect remained (t(25) = 1.81, p = 0.08), though only approaching significance due to limited power.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C39, C48-C49 address alternative explanations through design controls and additional analyses. The experimental design appropriately matched confounding variables (C37-C38), and the control analysis (C39) provides supporting evidence despite reduced power. The timing argument (C48) further supports the interpretation.

results.result: Previously encountering a sentence ending with the expected final word did not inflate spatial similarity between sentence pairs predicting the same word. A repeated measures ANOVA showed no main effect of order (F(1,25) = 0.747, p = 0.396) and no interaction (F(1,25) = 1.804, p = 0.191).
results.evaluation: Claim C40 addresses a potential memory confound with appropriate statistical analysis. The lack of order effects and interactions provides strong evidence that the spatial similarity effect is not driven by memory for previously encountered words. The ANOVA design is appropriate for this question.

results.result: The spatial similarity effect was not simply due to prediction of syntactic category. Spatial similarity for pairs predicting the same specific words was significantly larger than for pairs predicting the same syntactic category (t(25) = −3.559, p = 0.002), indicating the effect reflects lexico-semantic rather than purely syntactic predictions.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42, C53 address whether the effect reflects syntactic versus semantic predictions. The comparison between within-pair and within-category similarity is well-designed and statistically significant. This control analysis strengthens the interpretation that the effect reflects item-specific semantic predictions rather than broader syntactic categories.

results.result: The spatial patterns associated with prediction changed over time, as evidenced by the absence of off-diagonal effects in the cross-temporal similarity matrix. The spatial similarity effect was transient, lasting from 120-515 ms after SFW-1 onset before dropping off.
results.evaluation: Claims C43, C61, C64 describe the temporal dynamics of the spatial patterns. The cross-temporal analysis (C43) provides appropriate evidence for dynamic spatial patterns, and the timing information (C61) is clearly documented. These findings are well-supported by the data shown in Figure 2D.

results.result: Temporal RSA revealed that the temporal pattern of neural activity was more similar when sentence pairs predicted the same versus different words over central and posterior sensors (cluster-based randomization test: p = 0.002), indicating that prediction of specific words is associated with unique temporal patterns of neural activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C44 and C66 describe the main temporal RSA finding at the sensor level. The cluster-based permutation approach appropriately controls for multiple comparisons, and the statistical significance is clearly reported. This finding complements the spatial RSA results and is well-supported by the data in Figure 3A.

results.result: Source localization revealed that the temporal similarity effect localized to the left inferior temporal gyrus, extending into the medial temporal lobe including the left fusiform, hippocampus, and parahippocampus, as well as left cerebellum (p = 0.006).
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C45, C76, C90 describe the source localization of the temporal similarity effect. The beamforming approach is appropriate for MEG source localization, and the statistical significance is clearly reported with proper correction for multiple comparisons. The anatomical specificity is well-documented in Figure 3B.

results.result: The study provides neural evidence that item-specific lexico-semantic predictions are associated with unique spatial and temporal patterns of neural activity. This distinguishes the current work from previous studies that averaged across different predicted words.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C52, C88 state the main conclusion of the study. This conclusion is well-supported by the convergent evidence from both spatial RSA (C32, C46) and temporal RSA (C44, C45) analyses, along with appropriate control analyses ruling out alternative explanations. The novelty claim (C52) is justified given the experimental design.

results.result: The authors suggest that the unique spatial patterns reflected the prediction of spatially distributed semantic features associated with predicted words, with different predicted words activating different spatially distributed networks corresponding to their semantic features.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C54-C55, C60 present interpretations about semantic feature representations. While consistent with the data and prior literature (C26), these claims are largely speculative (as acknowledged in evidence_type). The study cannot definitively distinguish semantic from phonological/orthographic representations (C56-C57), limiting confidence in this specific interpretation.

results.result: The authors suggest that the left inferior/medial temporal lobe played a role in temporally 'binding' distributed semantic features through unique temporal patterns, consistent with Damasio's (1989) theory of temporal synchrony within convergence zones.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C69-C72 propose a temporal binding mechanism. While the temporal similarity effect is well-documented (C44-C45), the functional interpretation as 'binding' is speculative (as acknowledged in evidence_type). The consistency with Damasio's theory (C69) provides theoretical support, but the study does not directly test binding mechanisms or demonstrate causal relationships.

results.result: The increased spatial similarity may have reflected predictions at phonological and/or orthographic levels, potentially through top-down pre-activation from semantic to lower linguistic levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57 present an alternative interpretation of the spatial similarity effect. The authors acknowledge this possibility but note the study cannot distinguish between semantic and phonological/orthographic contributions due to the one-to-one correspondence between semantic features and word forms. This represents a limitation that requires future work to resolve.

results.result: The spatial similarity effect began at 120 ms after SFW-1 onset, suggesting predictions were generated as soon as sufficient information was available. This is consistent with generative frameworks where comprehenders predict events and semantic features prior to bottom-up input.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59 interpret the timing of the effect within a theoretical framework. The timing observation (120 ms) is well-documented (C32, C46), and the interpretation that this reflects the earliest point of unambiguous prediction is reasonable given the experimental design. The connection to generative frameworks (C59) is appropriately supported by citations.

results.result: The transient nature of the spatial similarity effect may reflect either lack of maintenance over the long interstimulus interval or 'activity-silent' working memory. Different semantic features may have been recruited at different time points, contributing to the dynamic spatial patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C63, C65 offer speculative interpretations of the transient effect. While the transient nature is well-documented (C61), the explanations are explicitly speculative. The activity-silent memory hypothesis (C63) is cited from prior work but not directly tested. The dynamic recruitment of features (C65) is plausible but remains speculative without direct evidence.

results.result: The findings extend previous work showing that temporal patterns in the left inferior temporal lobe encode item-specific representations during picture naming (Chen et al., 2016) by demonstrating that such patterns can be detected before new bottom-up input becomes available.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 position the findings relative to prior work. The citation to Chen et al. (2016) is appropriate, and the claim that the current findings extend this work by showing anticipatory temporal patterns is well-supported by the temporal RSA results (C44-C45). The novelty claim is justified.

results.result: The localization of the temporal similarity effect to left ventral temporal regions is consistent with the well-established role of these regions in lexico-semantic processing and their proposed function as semantic 'hubs' that integrate distributed semantic features.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75 interpret the anatomical localization within the context of prior literature. The localization finding is well-documented (C45), and the consistency with prior work on these regions' roles in semantic processing is appropriately supported by multiple citations. The interpretation as semantic hubs is well-grounded in the literature.

results.result: The possible involvement of the hippocampus is consistent with its role in binding representations to generate predictions, as demonstrated in rodent spatial navigation and human studies. The hippocampus may play an analogous role in language prediction.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C82 discuss hippocampal involvement. While the source localization shows medial temporal lobe activity (C76), the authors appropriately note that MEG source localization in deep structures should be interpreted with caution. The connection to prior work on hippocampal prediction is well-cited (C78-C82), but the inference about language prediction (C81) remains speculative given the methodological limitations.

results.result: The activity included the left cerebellum, which may play a role in generating item-specific predictions in language processing, though previous studies reported bilateral (right-dominant) cerebellar activation during language prediction.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 discuss cerebellar involvement. The source localization shows left cerebellar activity (C83), but this differs from prior reports of bilateral activation (C84). The interpretation that the cerebellum plays a role in item-specific predictions (C85) is speculative and should be interpreted cautiously given MEG's limited spatial resolution for deep structures.

results.result: The study deliberately used highly constraining contexts and long interstimulus intervals to encourage high-certainty predictions and ensure detection of representationally specific activity. The study does not address whether such predictions occur under more naturalistic conditions or whether they are probabilistic.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 acknowledge important limitations of the study design. The authors appropriately recognize that their experimental conditions were optimized for detecting item-specific predictions but do not speak to debates about prediction under more naturalistic conditions. This honest assessment of scope is important for interpreting the findings.

results.result: In conclusion, unique spatial patterns of neural activity became active around 100 ms after a word was unambiguously predicted with transient and dynamic activation, accompanied by unique temporal patterns localizing to the left inferior and medial temporal lobe.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C90 summarize the main findings. These conclusions are well-supported by the spatial RSA results (C32, C46, C61) and temporal RSA results (C44-C45). The summary accurately reflects the key empirical findings without overstating the interpretations.

results.result: A stimulus set of 120 sentence pairs in Mandarin was developed with highly constraining contexts (mean constraint: 88% ± 12%). Pairs had distinct contexts with no common content words (except 5 pairs) but predicted the same final word. Half predicted nouns and half predicted verbs. Stimuli were validated through cloze norming in 30 participants.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C95 describe the stimulus development and validation. The cloze norming procedure (C94) is appropriate for validating constraint, and the high mean constraint (C95) confirms the stimuli were suitable for encouraging specific predictions. The balanced design with nouns and verbs (C93) enables the syntactic control analysis (C41-C42).

results.result: The study was approved by the IRB of the Institute of Psychology, Chinese Academy of Sciences. Thirty-four participants were recruited, with 8 excluded due to technical problems, leaving 26 participants (mean age 23 years, 13 males) in the final dataset.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C98 describe ethical approval and participant information. The sample size (N=26) is reasonable for MEG studies, and the exclusion criteria (technical problems) are appropriate. The demographic information is adequately reported.

results.result: MEG data were collected using a CTF Omega System with 275 axial gradiometers (6 non-functional sensors excluded), with signals low-pass filtered at 300 Hz and digitized at 1200 Hz. After artifact rejection, 96% ± 3.4% of trials were retained on average.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C102 describe the MEG data acquisition and preprocessing. The equipment specifications are standard, the filtering and sampling parameters are appropriate, and the high trial retention rate (C102) indicates good data quality. The methods are sufficiently detailed for replication.

results.result: Prior work establishes that prediction is a core computational principle of brain function, that probabilistic prediction facilitates language comprehension, and that semantic features of upcoming words can be predicted in highly constraining contexts. Previous studies showed anticipatory brain activity but averaged across different predicted words, leaving unclear whether item-specific predictions produce unique neural patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C14 review prior literature and identify the research gap. The citations appropriately support the background claims about prediction in language processing (C7-C13). The identification of the gap (C14) is accurate and well-motivated, providing clear justification for the current study.

results.result: Multivariate Pattern Analysis (MVPA) and Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) provide methods for identifying unique patterns of neural activity. These approaches have been successfully applied to fMRI, MEG, and EEG data to decode representationally specific information during perception and working memory. Semantic features are thought to be represented in spatially distributed networks detectable with spatial RSA.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C20, C26 describe the methodological approach and its theoretical basis. The citations appropriately support the use of RSA methods (C15-C20), and the theoretical framework about distributed semantic representations (C26) is well-grounded in prior literature. This provides solid methodological justification for the study.

results.result: The authors interpret the spatial similarity effect as reflecting greater similarity in brain activity produced by predicting the same versus different words. While previous studies showed anticipatory lexico-semantic processing, the current study uniquely demonstrates that these predictions are item-specific with spatially distinct neural patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C47, C50-C51 present the authors' interpretation of their main finding. The interpretation (C47) is reasonable given the experimental design and control analyses. The positioning relative to prior work (C51) is accurate, and the claim of novelty (C52, included in another result) is justified by the unique experimental approach.
